bibliography.checked_against: the report's cover (page image) and the UWDC catalogue record
bibliography.note: Wisconsin DNR Research Report 111, September 1981, 12 pages; title as cited. Printed page = PDF page − 1 (PDF p. 1 is the library's cover sheet)

claims.claim: nests 0.8 m deep in a Maine lake (Forbes 1981)
claims.location: p. 2 (PDF p. 3), Spawning site characteristics: Location and Depth
claims.quote: 0.8 m deep in South Branch Lake, Maine (Neves 1975)
claims.conditions: a review: the value is Neves (1975), South Branch Lake
claims.note: cite as 'Neves 1975, via Forbes 1981' and name the lake

claims.claim: nests reach at least 71 per kilometer of suitable shore at Big Lake, Maine (Watson 1955, via Forbes 1981)
claims.location: p. 3 (PDF p. 4), Nest Size and Spacing of Nests (checked on the page image)
claims.quote: 4,218 nests were built along 59.5 km of suitable shoreline in Big Lake, Maine
claims.conditions: 'At least 4,218 nests' along 59.5 km of suitable (not total) shoreline; Watson 1955
claims.note: 4,218 / 59.5 km = 70.9 ≈ 71 nests/km; 'at least' is the source's

claims.claim: "It is generally agreed that unguarded nests will fail" (Forbes 1981)
claims.location: p. 4 (PDF p. 5), causes of nest failure: Nest Desertion
claims.quote: it is generally agreed that unguarded nests will fail
claims.conditions: Forbes cites Rawson 1945, Mraz 1960, Latta 1963 and Neves 1975 for it
claims.note: the same sentence opens with a qualification: nests without males have been observed to produce fry (Webster 1954)

claims.claim: named predators of unguarded nests include carp, suckers, white perch and crayfish (Forbes 1981)
claims.location: p. 4 (PDF p. 5), causes of nest failure: Predation
claims.quote: Carp, common suckers, white perch, and crayfish are known predators.
claims.conditions: summarized from Webster 1954, Latta 1963, Wiegert 1966 and Carlander 1977; the paragraph covers unguarded nests and predation 'in spite of male guardianship'
claims.note: Forbes names them as nest predators generally, not of unguarded nests only; carp, suckers and white perch also destroy nests mechanically (Bottom Disturbance)

claims.claim: Katherine Lake, Michigan (19.4 ha): deposited egg to autumn fingerling 1–4 % (Clady 1975, via Forbes 1981)
claims.location: p. 3 (PDF p. 4), First year survival: Nest Success; lake area in Nest Size and Spacing of Nests
claims.quote: from deposited egg to fall fingerling was 1-4%
claims.conditions: Clady 1975; Katherine Lake '19.4-ha', northern Michigan; 73–90 nests a year in 1967–69

claims.note: Forbes gives the lake's area and nest counts but says nothing of its colour; the description must come from Clady 1975 or another source

claims.claim: after dispersal the fry live singly or in small groups, in shallow water among stones or sticks and avoiding weed beds (Hubbs & Bailey 1938, via Forbes 1981)
claims.source_value: solitary after dispersal (no small groups); prefer shallow water, seek recesses around stones or sticks, avoid weed beds or dense brush; cited to Hubbs & Bailey 1938 and Hubbs & Eschmeyer 1938
claims.quote: Smallmouth bass are solitary after dispersal.
claims.conditions: review of older literature; before dispersal they 'rise from the nest in schools'
claims.note: 'or in small groups' is not in Forbes; the 28-mm dispersal length in the same sentence is not Forbes's either (not attributed to it). Forbes has the male near the fry for 7–10 days after hatching

claims.claim: young smallmouth solitary after dispersal, in recesses among stones near the nest; < 5 cm fish over sand and rock near shore (Forbes 1981's review)
claims.quote: less than 5 cm long were observed in shallow water over sandy and rocky bottoms
claims.conditions: the < 5 cm observation is Oneida Lake (Adams & Hankinson 1928), 'close to the shore or the margins of weedbeds'; 'slowly disperse and seek nearby cover'
claims.note: the same paragraph adds that Oneida young of the year, though densest inshore, occurred at 4.6–6.1 m (Forney 1972)

script-rendered shell, no text in the HTML

notes: Useful values for the rewrite: nest-success estimates in lakes range 44–86 % (Table 1; the paper's §3.6.2 quotes Steinhart's 44–96 %); Clady 1975 at Katherine Lake: 15–34 % of potential eggs deposited, 26–33 % deposited egg to postlarva, 1–4 % to fall fingerling (the paper cites Clady 1975 directly for the first two; if Clady was not read, they are 'via Forbes 1981'); Forbes cites Latta (1963), not 1957, for 28 % deposited egg to postlarva; nest construction and spawning begin at about 15.0–15.7 °C; eggs and new fry suffer if water drops below 14–15 °C and males may desert below 15.7 °C (Rawson 1945, Latta 1963); nest depths in lakes usually < 2 m (0.4–1.2 m in several lakes; most 1.8–3.0 m, some to 6.1 m, in Lake Geneva, Wisconsin), suitable depth 'related to water clarity'; MacLean et al. (1980) model: young bass < 5 cm less likely to survive their first winter, confirmed by Opeongo length distributions (Aug 1976 vs May 1977). Table 1's layout text drops the Tadenac and South Branch values; read them on the page image (PDF p. 5) if needed.
